Methods for storing and blending SAF are a function of fuel handling requirements, terminal operations, and the preferences of fuel suppliers and end users. Currently, SAF and Jet A are stored in separate tanks, where they are both tested for compliance with ASTM D7566 and ASTM D1655, respectively. SAF and Jet A are delivered in the desired ratio to a third blending tank, where the fuel is tested and certified as ASTM D1655 (Figure 19). A second option, not in use today, would deliver SAF directly to Jet A tanks for blending, where the fuel would be tested and certified as ASTM D1655. European best practices dictate that SAF use dedicated infrastructure for this second option (Energy Institute 2025). This second option, if enabled in the future, could be more economical and reduce the tankage necessary for blending SAF and Jet A. 27 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Current method of blending Jet A and SAF at a terminal. 2.1.4 SAF Projected Demand and Production Forecast Future Jet A and SAF demand and production data assumes continued growth in air travel. The Federal Aviation Administration projected that U.S. jet fuel demand will reach 34 billion gallons per year by 2050 (Federal Aviation Administration 2021). The EIA projects 2050 global jet fuel demand of 22.35 quadrillion Btu (equivalent to 165 billion gallons) (EIA 2023a). SkyNRG’s 2025 SAF Market Outlook projects a 2050 global jet fuel demand of 154 billion gallons (SkyNRG 2025). Various SAF demand predictions are shown in Figure 20. SkyNRG’s study also projects SAF demand based on various policy scenarios, including “existing policies,” which assumes existing mandates are met; “current trends,” which assumes the addition of targets being met; and “accelerated actions,” which assumes additional policies that aim toward net-zero goals (SkyNRG 2025). A caveat is that demand projections are based on policies that often reflect a percent of Jet A demand; some fuel policies are flexible and can be met by SAF and other biofuels, and global policy is evolving (SkyNRG 2025).
